newsitem.title: FRANCE: French farm minister welcomes milk agreement.
newsitem.headline: French farm minister welcomes milk agreement.

text.p: France's farm minister Philippe Vasseur welcomed a domestic agreement on milk reached on Wednesday which ends a row that had sparked farmers' protests across the country.
Vasseur vowed to defend the interests of the French dairy sector at European level, notably the export rebate system.
"I am very pleased by this accord that was difficult to reach," said Vasseur, who acted as a mediator in the marathon talks between dairy farmers, milk distributors and processors.
Wednesday's accord freezes the price farmers receive for their milk until end August at last year's levels of 1.70 to two francs per litre, depending on regions.
Last week, dairy farmers blocked deliveries to hypermarkets in various parts of France, accusing big distribution firms of pushing down milk prices.

Processors had wanted farmers to accept a two percent drop in the price of milk, arguing the cut was needed to make up for lower prices further down the delivery chain while farmers supported the freeze.
Last Wednesday a first round of government-sponsored talks had failed and Vasseur had accused industrial milk companies of blocking the talks.
As a result of the deal distributors will pay more for milk supplies but consumers should not feel the impact of the price rise in stores, distributors said.
"Processors will slightly raise the price they charge distributors, who will make a little less money," an official for the FNPL dairy farmers federation said.
The EU's 30-year old CAP regime is up for discussion this autumn amid calls by the EU's executive commission for price reductions under the existing regime of production quotas.

But EU farm ministers, who met for informal talks in the Netherlands earlier this week favour only a modest reform of the dairy regime. A majority of countries led by Germany want to extend the milk quota system when it expires at the end of March 2000.
